To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

business methods patents: (1) are no more or less likely to be granted than other data processing and software patents, (2) have the same number of claims as other data processing patents, (3) have the same average number of prior art citations as other data processing and computer software patents, and (4) have a higher average number of prior non-patent citations than computer software patents and a lower average number of prior patent citations than computer software, but not data processing, patents.

(1) the average number of claims in data processing, software and internet patents has increased over time, (2) the average number and proportion of prior art citations has increased over time for data processing patents, but decreased over time for internet patents, (3) the proportion of data processing patents citing prior art has increased over time and (4) data processing patents have a higher proportion of prior art and non-patents citations than other types of patents.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a particular type of patent - business method patents, and the quality of those patents.
the quality of patents on methods of conducting business.
the question of whether patents on methods of data processing are qualitatively different than other data processing and computer related patents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the quality of business method patents is not significantly different from the average quality of other data processing patents.
the data processing patents are no worse than the average data processing patents.

the data processing patents are not significantly different from the average patent in terms of prior art and claim breadth, but that they may be significantly different from the data processing patents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the data processing, software and internet patents are no more or less likely to cite prior art than other patents.
business method patents are not qualitatively different than other patents.
business method patents are not significantly different from other data processing patents in their citation and claim behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that
business method patents are not as bad as they are made out to be.
the data processing patent population is not a monolithic entity, and that the quality of patents within this population varies considerably.
the patent system, at least as measured by these three statistics, is working well.
